summary:
The Wealden iron industry operated in south-eastern England, using local ironstone and charcoal made from woodland. It was a major source of English bar iron in the 16th century and supplied most British cannon until about 1770.

Ironmaking began before the Roman conquest, expanded under Roman rule, then largely ceased until the ninth century. Water-powered bloomeries appeared from about the 14th century, and blast furnaces and finery forges arrived around 1490. Nearly 180 sites used these technologies between the 15th and 18th centuries. The industry peaked in the late 16th century, then lost markets for bar iron to Midland and imported Swedish iron, increasingly focusing on cannon.

After the Seven Years’ War, Wealden ironworks could not compete with cheaper coke-fired production. Because the Weald lacked accessible coal, the industry dwindled, and Ashburnham forge was the last to close.

Wealden bar iron lost markets to Midland iron; the points say only that the sale of Midland ironware may have marked the start of the decline in the London market.
Wealden bar iron definitively lost markets to imported Swedish iron; the points say it appears to have been unable to compete in London.
